name: New South Wales (British colony)
overview: The atlas shows New South Wales as an exact British-colony layer from 1878 to 1900, but those are map-coverage dates. The colony had responsible government from 1856 and became an Australian state on 1 January 1901. Its coarse polygon covers Sydney, Broken Hill, and the future Canberra site, excludes sampled Albury, and overlays many enduring Aboriginal Countries rather than mapping them. During these decades, wool, mining, farming, ports, railways, newspapers, schools, hospitals, and Sydney waterworks expanded. Growth was uneven: urban terraces, country homes, reserves, missions, mining camps, farms, and wealthy households offered sharply different daily lives. Children combined school, chores, work, reading, and play. Women sustained households, earned wages, printed newspapers, and organized for a vote they had not yet won. Chinese communities built businesses and associations while racist laws restricted migration and reunion. The Aborigines Protection Board extended colonial control over reserves, rations, schooling, work, and families. Strikes, depression, bank failures, and disease exposed insecurity. Federation campaigns eventually succeeded, but the atlas repaint at 1900 is one year early and no ending for people, families, languages, or Country.

periods.title: 1878 to 1880: An atlas label and an international exhibition
periods.summary: The exact colonial id first appears in 1878, although New South Wales had responsible government long before then. Sydney opened the Garden Palace exhibition in September 1879, drawing more than one million visits across seven months and displaying art, machinery, manufactures, and technologies from many countries and colonies.

periods.title: 1880 to 1883: Schools and public health expand
periods.summary: The Public Instruction Act came into force in 1880, creating compulsory attendance and new public-school forms while retaining fees and unequal access. Sydney’s 1881 smallpox outbreak exposed harsh quarantine conditions and helped produce a Board of Health, notification rules, an ambulance service, and an infectious-disease hospital.

periods.title: 1883 to 1885: Protection administration and Broken Hill grow
periods.summary: The government created the Aborigines Protection Board in 1883 with paternalistic aims and increasing influence over reserves and daily lives. That same year, a mineral claim on Wiljakali Country began Broken Hill’s mining boom; rich silver ore and the registration of BHP followed in 1885.

periods.title: 1885 to 1889: Empire, rail, water, and argument
periods.summary: New South Wales sent a colonial contingent under British command to Sudan in 1885, amid celebration and opposition. Railway construction connected more towns, and the 1888 water authority and Upper Nepean scheme strengthened Sydney’s supply. These projects expanded state capacity without making benefits equal across the colony.

periods.title: 1889 to 1891: Federation and labor politics enter public debate
periods.summary: Henry Parkes appealed publicly for Federation at Tenterfield in October 1889. The maritime strike of 1890 failed against coordinated employers and government power, encouraging unionists to pursue parliamentary action. In 1891 the Labor Electoral League won thirty-five New South Wales seats and the first federal convention met in Sydney.

periods.title: 1891 to 1894: Depression deepens while women organize
periods.summary: A severe depression followed the property boom; investment collapsed, banks failed, and unemployment strained families and charities. The Womanhood Suffrage League formed in New South Wales in 1891. Women petitioned, published, spoke, and organized, but the colonial franchise still denied them the vote during this period.

periods.title: 1894 to 1898: Recovery is uneven and a constitution returns
periods.summary: Economic conditions slowly improved, though drought and lost savings prolonged hardship. Federation conventions resumed in 1897 and 1898. New South Wales voters gave the draft constitution a simple majority in 1898, but the enabling law demanded eighty thousand yes votes, so the proposal did not yet pass there.

periods.title: 1898 to 1900: Voters approve Federation and the atlas repaints
periods.summary: After amendments, a second New South Wales referendum in 1899 approved Federation by a larger majority. Britain enacted the Constitution law in July 1900. The atlas removes this exact id at 1900 and temporarily uses a broad United Kingdom layer, although the constitutional change began on 1 January 1901.

sections.title: Read a colonial polygon without mistaking it for Country

items.text: The imported record calls New South Wales a UK state from 1878 to 1900. The id is absent from the 1815 control; those dates describe two atlas layers, not the colony’s founding or legal ending. When this packet began, the id lacked both a card and reviewed override, so its modern summary could not safely fill the gap.

The decoded 1878 polygon has one ring with 57 positions and a bounding box from about 140.976 to 153.493 degrees east and 38.005 to 28.132 degrees south. It is a global-atlas approximation of colonial jurisdiction, not a cadastral survey, title deed, or magical fence.

The 1880 polygon also has 57 positions and identical tested membership, but tiny coordinate drift gives it a different hash. Sydney, Newcastle, Broken Hill, Tenterfield, and the future Canberra site test inside. Sampled Albury tests outside, exposing a simplified southern edge rather than a nineteenth-century border correction.

In both snapshots the encoded polygon shares arcs with Queensland, Victoria, and South Australia. Shared arcs reveal how this dataset partitions mainland space. They cannot prove peaceful possession, consent, exact surveying, cultural uniformity, or that every colonial office exercised equal power from Sydney to the far west.

New South Wales contains many Aboriginal Nations, languages, clans, and Countries with enduring responsibilities to land and water. A modern educational map offers broad names and locations, not fixed legal borders. The colonial polygon overlays those relationships; it does not combine them into one people or replace their authority.

sections.title: See how colonial government worked, and whom it excluded

items.text: Responsible government meant ministers depended on the elected Legislative Assembly, while a governor represented the Crown and an appointed Legislative Council reviewed laws. The arrangement gave settlers substantial local government under British sovereignty. It did not make the colony independent or settle Indigenous sovereignty by parliamentary procedure.

Women could not vote in colonial New South Wales, even as suffragists held meetings, petitioned, wrote, and lobbied. South Australia and Western Australia enfranchised women earlier. New South Wales women won state voting rights only in 1902, so Federation debate did not mean equal political membership.

Politics initially revolved around shifting personal factions, then organized Free Trade and Protectionist groupings became clearer. Governments built railways, waterworks, schools, and postal systems while moving cautiously on health, welfare, and working conditions. Public capacity expanded, but budgets and benefits followed political power and geography.

The colony raised about 770 troops for Sudan at its own expense, under British command. Crowds cheered their departure, while working-class suburbs and country miners also expressed opposition. The episode shows imperial loyalty and growing colonial confidence together, with disease causing deaths even though the contingent saw little fighting.

Colonial immigration law imposed taxes and ship limits on Chinese arrivals in 1881, raised its tax and tightened its ship limit in 1887, and added an 1898 dictation test aimed at non-Europeans. These laws shaped family reunion, travel, work, and belonging. Federation later inherited exclusionary machinery.

sections.title: Move wool, ore, people, money, and political ideas

items.text: Wool remained enormously important, while wheat, fruit, sugar, dairying, refrigeration, and mining broadened production. Railways connected farms, mines, towns, and ports, but expansion also served settler occupation and debt-financed development. Economic totals describe colonial markets; they do not measure dispossession or unpaid household work.

Under engineer John Whitton, the railway network grew from 37 kilometres in 1856 to about 3,495 kilometres in 1899. Bridges and viaducts used local stone where budgets discouraged imported iron. Trains shortened journeys and moved freight, yet branch access, fares, timetables, and safety varied widely.

On Wiljakali Country, claims pegged in 1883 led to rich silver, lead, and zinc discoveries and BHP’s formation in 1885. Broken Hill grew rapidly into a mining town with workers, businesses, migrants, unions, dust, and technical hazards. “Achievement” includes ore processing and organization, not a free pass for damage.

The 1890 maritime and 1891 shearers strikes mobilized workers across colonies but were defeated by employers, police, money, and replacement labor. Unionists then pursued elections; the Labor Electoral League won thirty-five New South Wales seats in 1891. A lost strike helped build a new political strategy.

Property speculation, weaker lending, falling investment, and lost British capital fed the 1890s depression. The financial crisis peaked in 1893, when many institutions suspended or closed. Households faced unemployment and inaccessible savings. Bank reconstruction repaired balance sheets more neatly than it repaired a family dinner.

sections.title: Enter homes, kitchens, workshops, and boarding houses

items.text: Meroogal, built at Nowra in 1886, preserves one women-led household with gardens, orchard, chickens, diaries, visitors, charity work, washing days, baking, preserving, and rented rooms. It reveals resourceful daily life without standing for a miner’s hut, crowded Sydney terrace, Aboriginal camp, or Chinese boarding house.

Surry Hills mixed small factories, laundries, yards, shops, pubs, schools, and tightly packed housing. Women sewed clothing through outwork and piecework to support family incomes. Poor drainage and overcrowding harmed health. The suburb’s streets placed paid production and domestic labor almost on each other’s doorstep.

Museum kitchens and dining collections show wood stoves, cookbooks, gardens, servants, family labor, preserving, tea tables, and formal meals across households of very different means. Food history therefore needs class and place attached. A silver service and a working kitchen tell related stories, not identical breakfasts.

Domestic manuals offered advice about thrift, cooking, home medicine, etiquette, dress, needlework, servants, and care of animals. They reveal ideals and anxieties, especially for literate households able to buy or borrow them. Instructions show what authors wanted done, not proof that every saucepan obeyed.

Sydney’s Chinese community included merchants, market gardeners, cooks, furniture workers, shopkeepers, boarders, women, children, and clan associations. Stores could provide letters, remittances, dispute help, and burial arrangements. Restrictive law and racism mattered, but community history is larger than the prejudice directed at it.

sections.title: Meet families, women, neighbors, and public campaigns

items.text: The women of Meroogal combined heavy housework with social calls, local charities, reading, gardens, correspondence, and family decision-making. Their home depended on kin support, property, and careful thrift. That record complicates both the idle Victorian lady and the lonely bush household, while remaining one family’s experience.

Louisa Lawson moved from rural working life into Sydney publishing and political activism. Urban factories and workshops were opening more wage work to women, though domestic service remained important. Marriage, household size, and paid work varied by class; “women stayed home” is an ideal, not a census result.

The Dawn began in 1888 as a journal owned, edited, typeset, and printed by women. It discussed work, clothing, health, marriage, law, and suffrage. A printing press became both employment and political infrastructure, proving that household questions could walk straight into public argument wearing printer’s ink.

Suffragists organized leagues, rallies, petitions, speeches, newspaper campaigns, deputations, and parliamentary lobbying. New South Wales bills repeatedly failed before 1902. Political exclusion did not mean political silence: women created networks and arguments that changed public life before the ballot paper finally caught up.

Family life crossed languages, religions, origins, and legal categories. Immigration restrictions could separate Chinese residents from relatives or complicate return after travel. Colonial records often count adult male workers most clearly, so the archive can make women, children, friendships, and care networks look smaller than they were.

sections.title: Send children to school, work, play, and institutional care

items.text: The Public Instruction Act required children aged six to fourteen to attend at least seventy days each half-year. Enrolment rose sharply, but fees, distance, work, illness, floods, and discrimination still interrupted attendance. “Compulsory” described a legal duty; it did not teleport every child into a desk.

The statute created public, provisional, half-time, evening, superior, and high schools. It capped weekly public-school fees, allowed remission for families unable to pay, and even permitted free railway passes to the nearest school. The law’s detail shows administrators solving distance with timetables, petitions, and paperwork.

Sydney Boys High and Sydney Girls High opened in 1883, while Catholic schools continued without state aid. Fees and examinations shaped access. Working-class children still contributed wages and chores, so formal schooling competed with household need rather than instantly replacing children’s economic roles.

Children worked in shops, streets, homes, and family businesses; they also read expanding books and magazines, played games, attended church, and visited spectacles. Nearly 28,000 exhibition visitors arrived on one January 1880 holiday, many of them children. Childhood differed sharply by money, gender, health, and neighborhood.

The 1881 State Children Relief system expanded boarding-out, placing destitute children with supervised families instead of large institutions. By 1886 more than 1,300 had been boarded out. Outcomes varied, and “rescue” records carry official judgments about poverty, respectability, work, discipline, and whose home counted as suitable.

sections.title: Face illness with home care, hospitals, nurses, and public health

items.text: Sydney’s smallpox outbreak involved 154 notified cases and forty deaths across nine months. Families were removed to quarantine under frightening and sometimes miserable conditions. Public anger and investigation helped create a Board of Health, compulsory notification, trained ambulance arrangements, and a dedicated infectious-disease hospital at Little Bay.

NSW Health dates modern public-health administration to the smallpox crisis. Colonial responses linked doctors, police, quarantine, sanitation, notification, and government authority. These systems could control infection and also coerce households. Medical history must count institutional capacity and the experience of people subjected to it.

Prince Alfred Hospital opened in 1882 with wards, dispensary, outpatient care, staff quarters, and accident beds. Its formal operating theatre opened in 1887; by 1900 aseptic practice was reducing infection risk. Chloroform anaesthesia and hand washing marked change, though surgery remained dangerous and access unequal.

Hospitals, benevolent asylums, churches, charities, family care, and private doctors formed an uneven welfare landscape. Overcrowding and poor sanitation could make institutions unhealthy, while unemployed, aged, disabled, and poor residents feared dependence. A grand facade did not guarantee a clean ward or an affordable visit.

Prince Alfred Hospital’s 1882 pay scale distinguished probationers, nurses, sisters, and a matron, recording both professional hierarchy and women’s paid labor. Nursing demanded cleaning, observation, feeding, comfort, discipline, and long hours. Wages help recover work that celebratory hospital architecture can quietly hide behind the sandstone.

sections.title: Carry water, move sewage, and answer the toilet question

items.text: Sydney created a dedicated water and sewerage authority in 1888, when the Upper Nepean scheme linked rivers, canals, and reservoirs to strengthen metropolitan supply. That engineering achievement served a growing city, not every household in the colony. Rural towns, farms, camps, and reserves depended on very different arrangements.

In the late 1890s, southern, western, and northern sewerage systems began carrying wastewater to treatment works, while pumping stations followed from 1899. Construction reduced harbor discharge over time, but connection was uneven. A sewer on an engineer’s plan did not instantly remove every cesspit from a backyard.

Sydney bought cast-iron public urinals for men in 1880 and added more during the decade. Women workers and visitors had far fewer facilities. The technology is almost comically simple; the social lesson is not. Who could remain comfortably in public space depended partly on where one could pee.

Many inner-city houses still relied on earth closets or cesspits, and faulty or missing sewer connections became glaring during the 1900 plague response. Night-soil systems required workers, carts, access, and disposal sites. Toilets were infrastructure, labor, privacy, smell, money, and politics packed into one small room.

Meroogal’s preserved objects include a chamber pot, meat safe, wood stove, hand-pumped well water, and games. They make household technology tangible for children today. They also belong to one substantial 1886 Nowra home, so the chamber pot gets a label, not promotion to colony-wide bathroom ambassador.

sections.title: Keep Aboriginal Countries, families, and languages in view

items.text: Aboriginal Country connects law, place, language, custom, family, spiritual responsibility, and material life. New South Wales covered many distinct groups, never one Aboriginal population with a single border or practice. Even Indigenous mapping uses blurred, contested general locations and cannot authorize a colonial polygon as cultural ownership.

The Aborigines Protection Board was created in 1883 without an initial statutory act. Officials framed its work as protection, training, and aid, while records reveal growing surveillance of reserves, rations, work, schooling, and families. Paternalistic language belongs to the administrators who wrote it, not to neutral description.

The Board’s 1894 report lists station populations, adults, children, rations, buildings, cultivation, and officials through racial categories now recognized as harmful. It can document households and administration while still distorting people into columns. A government table is evidence about power as well as population.

At Brewarrina, authorities moved Aboriginal people to a reserve in 1885; a mission opened in 1886, and the Board assumed control in 1897. Recorded population remained far below the district count because many people did not live there. One institution cannot stand for all Aboriginal family, work, health, or education.

Nineteenth-century surveyors and missionaries recorded wordlists from many New South Wales languages. The lists preserve valuable traces but use outsider spelling, selection, and translation. They are not interchangeable, fully authoritative dictionaries, or permission to print one word as the colony’s Aboriginal language. Community knowledge must guide interpretation.

sections.title: Celebrate invention, culture, and words without hiding their costs

items.text: The Sydney International Exhibition opened in 1879 with displays from thirty-four countries and colonies, about fourteen thousand exhibits, and more than 1.1 million visits over seven months. Machinery, manufacturing, art, and handicrafts shared the building. Its steam tram later helped seed a wider urban network.

The Garden Palace burned in 1882, destroying government records, artworks, and cultural collections. The Australian Museum now acknowledges that many First Nations and Pacific objects displayed there had been taken without consent or under pressure. Scientific achievement and collecting violence occupy the same institutional history.

Sydney’s tram network grew from the exhibition line after Parliament authorized further construction in 1880. Steam, cable, and later electric systems moved workers, shoppers, and visitors between expanding suburbs and the center. The network changed city time and distance, while most rural residents remained well beyond its bell.

Pubs, race meetings, theaters, churches, picnics, clubs, kitchens, and sports created different social worlds. Respectability campaigns and amateur sport appealed strongly to sections of the middle class, while working-class leisure included gambling and drinking. Gender shaped access: a lively street could still be an uncomfortable place for women.

A securely dated colonial English sample comes from Parkes’s Tenterfield speech: “The great question which we have to consider is, whether the time has not now arisen”. Delivered on 24 October 1889 and reported in newspapers, it is public political English. It represents neither Aboriginal languages nor every colonial voice.

ending.text: The exact new-south-wales-uk id disappears at the atlas’s 1900 snapshot, when the same tested places move into a broad United Kingdom layer. That is an editorial repaint, not the precise constitutional event. The Commonwealth of Australia began on 1 January 1901 under the 1900 Constitution Act, and New South Wales changed from a British colony into an Australian state. Its Parliament continued, retaining major responsibilities while customs, defence, postage, and other powers moved to the Commonwealth. Federation did not erase towns, farms, unions, schools, businesses, families, or local institutions. It also did not surrender or extinguish Aboriginal Countries, laws, languages, kinship, and cultural authority, and the successor link cannot imply Indigenous consent to colonization. The atlas reaches an Australia layer by 1914. This card therefore ends with governmental transformation and social continuity: a colony changed constitutional status while the many peoples within and across its rough polygon continued, adapted, organized, resisted, cared, taught, worked, and created.
